questions.question: Q: How was Greek drama connected to religion and civic life?

points.text: Drama developed from choral hymns to Dionysus at the City Dionysia festival. The state organised dramatic competitions, citizens were expected to attend, and wealthy choregoi funded productions as a civic liturgy. Plays explored moral and political themes relevant to the polis, making theatre a form of public debate.

questions.question: Q: What were the contributions of the three great tragedians?

points.text: Aeschylus introduced the second actor, enabling dialogue and dramatic conflict (Persae, Oresteia). Sophocles added the third actor, painted scenery and larger choruses (Oedipus Rex, Antigone). Euripides questioned traditional values and portrayed complex, realistic characters (Medea, The Bacchae).

questions.question: Q: How did Aristophanes use comedy for political commentary?

points.text: Aristophanes wrote Old Comedy that directly satirised living politicians, generals and intellectuals. The Clouds mocked Socrates, The Wasps satirised jury-mad Athenians, and Lysistrata showed women ending war through a sex strike. Comedy was politically bold because of Athenian free speech (parrhesia).

questions.question: Q: What made the Parthenon architecturally significant?

points.text: Built 447-432 BC under Pericles, the Parthenon combined Doric and Ionic elements, used optical refinements (slight curves to counteract visual distortion), housed a massive gold-and-ivory statue of Athena, and displayed sculptural friezes celebrating Athenian mythology and civic pride. It symbolised Athenian power and cultural supremacy.

questions.question: Q: What was the role of the choregos in Greek theatre?

points.text: A choregos was a wealthy citizen assigned to finance a play's chorus as a liturgy (civic duty). This was expensive but brought prestige. The choregos paid for costumes, training and maintenance of the chorus. The best-funded production won a prize, creating competition among the elite.
